extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, rhetoric, and classical literature
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria from a Platonic dialogue (Gorgias) about what counts as true art/rhetoric and the relation between pleasure and the good; useful for judging speeches, arts, and ethical ends. Focuses on distinctions between flattery and noble rhetoric, art versus mere experience, and the health/order of the soul as a measure of goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric: two kinds — flattery versus noble rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric is of two sorts; one is mere flattery and disgraceful declamation which aims only at giving pleasure, the other is noble and aims at the training and improvement of the souls of the citizens, and strives to say what is best, whether welcome or unwelcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and contrasts: theatrical poetry, choral performance, and many popular orators are described as aiming at pleasure (flattery). A true rhetorician "who is honest and understands his art" should fix on justice, temperance and other virtues in his speech. Anti-pattern: addressing a crowd merely to delight them without regard to their true interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art versus mere experience (cookery vs medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: An art has principles, attends to the nature and constitution of its subject, and acts for the good of that subject; by contrast, an experience (e.g., cookery) aims only at pleasure and follows routine and recollection without consulting what is good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit criteria for calling something an art: it ‘knows’ good and evil in detail, has principles and reason for action, and seeks the true interest of the patient/subject. Anti-pattern: processes that pursue gratification without considering whether the gratification promotes the subject's true wellbeing (labelled "flattery"). Examples: medicine = art; cookery = experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: The good is distinct from pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is not the same as the good; some pleasures are beneficial (good) and others hurtful (evil). The argument uses examples (hunger/thirst and eating/drinking) and the fact that pleasure and pain can co-occur to show the good cannot be identified simply with pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: if a pleasure promotes health or excellence it is good; if it promotes harm it is evil. Logical anti-pattern: defining the good purely as whatever brings pleasure (leads to paradoxes where bad persons could be ‘‘better’’ by that standard). Use examples of pleasures that injure versus those that benefit to distinguish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beneficial versus hurtful pleasures (selection by effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures which promote health or other excellences are beneficial and therefore good; pleasures which are hurtful are evil. Similarly, there are good pains and evil pains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: choose and use the good pleasures and pains and avoid the evil ones. Example: bodily pleasures that promote health are good; those that damage health are bad. Implies an evaluative procedure: examine downstream effects on the subject's excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and harmony of the soul as measure of moral good (temperance and justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of order and harmony in the soul corresponds to moral excellence; just as harmony in a house or body is called health, harmony in the soul is expressed as lawfulness, temperance, and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical test: evaluate whether parts are harmonized and ordered (good) or in disorder (evil). Thus moral evaluation focuses on whether a speech/practice produces order/harmony (virtue) in souls rather than mere pleasurable states. Use as positive criterion: promotes temperance/justice = good.

rubrics_metrics.name: True rhetorician’s aim: implant virtue, not pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The honest rhetorician aims to implant justice and take away injustice, to implant temperance and take away intemperance, to implant every virtue and remove every vice — i.e., to improve the soul rather than merely to gratify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational guidance for evaluating rhetoric: prefer speeches that pursue the public good and moral improvement even if they are unwelcome; distrust speeches aimed primarily at pleasing the audience. Example/anti-pattern: orators who play the people like children, aiming to amuse rather than better them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattery defined as a process that seeks only pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Flattery (whether of body or soul) is any process employed with a view to pleasure and without consideration of good and evil — speech that delights an assembly while disregarding their true interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying flattery: speech addressed to a heterogeneous crowd seeking immediate gratification; arts (e.g., certain kinds of poetry, spectacle, oratory) that prioritize delight over moral result are failures. Use historical examples cited (tragedy, dithyrambic poetry, popular oratory) as anti-patterns when they avoid moral improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discerning good pleasures requires art/knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A person cannot reliably choose which pleasures are good or evil without art or knowledge; one must have expertise to distinguish beneficial from harmful pleasures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for practice: ethical choice is not merely preference or appetite — it requires trained judgment. Thus evaluation of policies, speeches or practices should rely on principled knowledge about consequences, not on surface pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint/chastisement can be beneficial when the soul is diseased
rubrics_metrics.description: When the soul is intemperate, senseless, unjust, or unholy (in a bad state), its desires ought to be controlled and chastised; such restraint is better for the soul than indulgence and leads to its improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to medicine: as physicians restrict a sick person's immediate satisfactions for long-term health, moral agents or educators should restrain intemperate souls for their improvement. Anti-pattern: treating every gratification as legitimate while neglecting corrective measures when disorder prevails.

rubrics_metrics.name: The good is the end of actions; pleasure is instrumentally sought for the good
rubrics_metrics.description: All actions are to be done for the sake of the good, not the good for the sake of actions; pleasure is to be sought for the sake of that which is good, not as the ultimate end itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative rule: judge actions/speeches by whether they pursue the true end (the good) and use pleasure only instrumentally. Policy implication: short-term pleasurable outcomes are insufficient criteria unless they contribute to the overall good.
